resident.chief_complaint: Progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, unsteady gait, and altered sensation of the feet described as 'walking on cotton wool'.
resident.history: 30-year-old male engineer of African descent presented with progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, associated with an unsteady gait. He reported altered sensation of his feet, described as 'walking on cotton wool'. He denied any preceding trauma and no neck or back pain.
resident.physical_exam: Normal power in both upper and lower limbs. Generalized hyper-reflexia in all muscle groups of both upper and lower limbs, bilateral inverted supinator jerk, positive Hoffman's sign, and clonus. Sensation decreased in the left sole of the foot, sparing the dorsum. Japanese Orthopaedic Association score 7; Nurick's Grading grade 3.
key_positive_signs: Generalized hyper-reflexia in all muscle groups of both upper and lower limbs
Decreased sensation in the left sole of the foot sparing the dorsum
MRI stenosis with cord signal changes C4-C6 from bony growth at C6 spinous process
resident.past_history: Denied any preceding trauma; no neck or back pain. No other past medical history documented.
resident.public_message: A 30-year-old male of African descent presented with progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness over 3 months, unsteady gait, and altered sensation of the feet described as 'walking on cotton wool'. Examination revealed normal power but generalized hyper-reflexia, bilateral inverted supinator jerk, positive Hoffman's sign, clonus, and decreased sensation in the left sole sparing the dorsum. JOA score was 7 and Nurick's grade 3. MRI of the whole spine showed stenosis with cord signal changes from C4 to C6 secondary to impingement by a bony growth from the C6 spinous process; CT confirmed the bony mass. These findings are reported as recorded.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; the films were not available for review. The record describes spinal canal stenosis with cord signal changes from C4-6 due to dorsal canal impingement by a prominent bony growth arising anterosuperiorly from the C6 spinous process. The record does not provide a stenosis grade. These findings correlate highly with the reported cervical myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical myelopathy involving upper motor neuron pathways secondary to C4-C6 dorsal cord compression; additional left S1-distribution sensory deficit suggests possible coexisting lumbosacral radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy.

red_flags.finding: Reported progressive left upper limb and bilateral lower limb weakness with normal power on examination.
red_flags.rationale: The reported weakness is not supported by objective motor examination; this may reflect subjective fatigue, early myelopathy without measurable power loss, or functional overlay. It does not offer an alternative explanation for the upper motor neuron signs and does not change the indication from cervical cord compression.

red_flags.finding: Decreased sensation in the left sole of the foot sparing the dorsum.
red_flags.rationale: This sensory pattern is not typical of cervical cord myelopathy (which would be bilateral or below a level) and suggests a peripheral process such as left S1 radiculopathy or distal neuropathy. It coexists rather than altering the cervical localization or indication.

red_flags.finding: JOA score 7 and Nurick grade 3 despite documented normal power in all limbs.
red_flags.rationale: The severe functional scores conflict with the normal motor examination. This discrepancy may indicate non-organic factors, cognitive/coordination issues, or imprecise scoring, but it does not negate the myelopathic signs. It warrants further clarification but does not change the causal role of the C4-C6 compression.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The C4-C6 dorsal compression and cord signal change explain the upper motor neuron signs, but the unilateral left sole sensory loss sparing the dorsum is not explained by this lesion; it suggests a coexisting left S1 or peripheral nerve process.
neurology.public_message: Localization is to the cervical spinal cord at C4-C6, matching the upper motor neuron findings. The imaging explains the dominant myelopathic syndrome. Red flags: (1) reported weakness but normal power — coexisting, does not change indication; (2) left S1-distribution sensory loss — coexisting, likely peripheral/radicular; (3) JOA 7/Nurick 3 with normal power — coexisting, needs clarification. Symptom-imaging mismatch: left sole sensory loss is not explained by cervical lesion.

anesthesia.public_message: The patient is a 30-year-old male with cervical myelopathy due to C4-C6 stenosis and a C6 bony growth causing cord compression. ASA physical status is III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target is 85 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk is moderate. Prone position tolerance is moderate given cervical cord compression and need for careful positioning. physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3 months initial, extendable to 6 months if stable or improving
preconditions_for_failure: Any decline in JOA score or Nurick grade during the trial
Appearance of new or worsening objective neurologic deficits (e.g., motor weakness, gait deterioration)
No improvement or stabilization of myelopathic symptoms after 3 months of structured rehabilitation
Progression of cord signal change on follow-up MRI at 3 months
Patient preference for surgery after informed discussion
physiatrist_opening.public_message: As the rehabilitation physician, I formally propose a conservative management trial: 3 months (extendable to 6 if stable or improving) of supervised physical therapy focused on gait, balance, core stabilization, and posture; activity modification; and close neurologic monitoring. The reported success rate for severe cervical myelopathy with cord signal change is modest (~30%), and I acknowledge the evidence that progressive myelopathy may warrant early surgical decompression to prevent irreversible cord damage. Therefore, this trial is only appropriate with strict preconditions: any decline in JOA/Nurick, new neurologic deficits, or progression of MRI signal change mandates immediate surgical referral. I am not yet persuaded that surgery must be the first step for this young patient, but I will concede if these conditions are met.

physiatrist_final.proposed_duration: 3 months initial, extendable to 6 months if stable or improving
preconditions_for_failure: JOA score declines by ≥1 point or Nurick grade increases by ≥1
New or worsening objective motor deficit (MRC grade <5) or gait deterioration
No stabilization or improvement after 3 months of structured rehabilitation
Progression of cord signal change on follow-up MRI at 3 months
Patient preference for surgery after informed discussion
physiatrist_final.public_message: I support the director's plan for further workup, but those studies are not yet part of the record, and no argument since my last statement has pointed to a specific finding I underweighted. I have already accounted for the progressive myelopathy and cord signal changes by making my conservative proposal conditional on strict failure criteria. To address the director's request: I would implement supervised physical therapy 2-3 times weekly focusing on gait, balance, core stabilization, and posture, with monthly neurologic reassessment using JOA and Nurick, and repeat MRI at 3 months. Immediate surgical referral would occur if any of the listed criteria are met. The deputy director's restatement of progressive myelopathy and cord signal change does not add weight beyond what I have already considered. My stance remains conditional: I accept surgery if any failure criterion is met during the trial, but I do not accept primary surgery as mandated by the current record.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 30-year-old male with progressive cervical myelopathy (JOA 7, Nurick 3) caused by dorsal cord compression from a bony lesion arising from the C6 spinous process, resulting in C4-C6 stenosis with cord signal change. The clinical picture is consistent with cervical cord dysfunction, though there are inconsistencies: reported weakness but normal power, left S1-distribution sensory loss not explained by the cervical lesion, and a relatively high JOA score despite normal power. Progressive myelopathy with cord signal change is a strong indication for surgical decompression to prevent irreversible cord damage. I acknowledge the physiatry proposal for a conservative trial, but I am concerned that delaying surgery in the face of cord signal change may risk permanent neurologic deterioration. Surgical decompression with lesion resection is my preferred option, while recognizing that the diagnostic ambiguities should be clarified either before or at surgery.
proposed_options: Surgical decompression: posterior approach with resection of the C6 spinous process bony lesion and cervical laminectomy/laminoplasty from C4 to C6, adding fusion if instability is present.
Conservative management: a structured 3-6 month trial of supervised physiotherapy with strict neurologic monitoring and predefined criteria for surgical referral (as outlined by physiatry).

Further diagnostic workup before a treatment decision: contrast-enhanced MRI, CT angiography to assess lesion vascularity, lumbar MRI/EMG for the left S1 sensory loss, and dynamic flexion-extension films to evaluate stability.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Surgical decompression: posterior approach with resection of the C6 spinous process bony lesion and cervical laminectomy/laminoplasty from C4 to C6, adding fusion if instability is present.
disagreement_points: Whether a conservative trial is acceptable given progressive myelopathy with cord signal change; I believe it carries a significant risk of irreversible cord injury and should not be the default.
The unexplained left S1-distribution sensory loss (not accounted for by the cervical lesion) and whether it warrants additional workup (lumbar MRI/EMG) before surgery.
The mismatch between reported subjective weakness and normal power on examination, and whether the JOA/Nurick scores accurately reflect current functional status.
Whether the bony lesion has been adequately characterized (e.g., with contrast MRI or CT angiography) to assess the risk of intraoperative bleeding or the need for preoperative biopsy/embolization.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that surgical decompression should be offered now rather than after a trial of conservative therapy?
Should we obtain further imaging (lumbar MRI/EMG, dynamic films, contrast MRI) before scheduling surgery, or can these be completed during the surgical admission?
Is there a role for a multidisciplinary tumor board or additional consultation given the unusual bony lesion, prior to committing to surgery?
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend surgical decompression and resection of the C6 bony lesion as the primary treatment, given the progressive myelopathy and cord signal changes. I hear the physiatry proposal for a conservative trial, but I am concerned that delay risks irreversible cord damage. I would like us to clarify the diagnostic ambiguities and agree on whether any further workup is needed before proceeding. I defer the final decision to the director.

vice_opinions.assessment: The progressive cervical myelopathy with cord signal changes from C4-C6 due to a dorsal bony lesion at C6 is the dominating problem. Although the neurological examination has some inconsistencies (reported weakness but normal power, left S1 sensory loss), the imaging description and symptom progression strongly indicate spinal cord compression requiring timely surgical decompression. I am not persuaded that a primary conservative trial is safe in the face of documented progression, although I acknowledge the physiatrist's strict preconditions. The director's decision to obtain further imaging and neurophysiology before finalizing a plan is prudent, especially to characterize the bony lesion and exclude a vascular or aggressive tumor. I will coordinate the requested tumor board review and provide specific advice on biopsy and embolization once the additional studies are available.
proposed_options: Proceed with surgical decompression and resection of the C6 bony lesion once the ordered investigations are complete and the tumor board has reviewed the case, with preoperative embolization if imaging suggests a vascular lesion.

If MRI contrast or CT suggests an aggressive or highly vascular lesion, obtain a tissue diagnosis via CT-guided biopsy before definitive surgery, or alternatively proceed directly to open resection with intraoperative frozen section.

Delay any surgical decision until all ordered tests (cervical MRI with contrast, lumbar MRI, dynamic flexion-extension films, lower limb EMG/NCS) are completed and reviewed, with close neurological monitoring and urgent surgery if deterioration occurs.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Proceed with surgical decompression and resection after completing the requested investigations and tumor board review, with preoperative embolization if imaging suggests a vascular lesion.
disagreement_points: Whether a conservative trial with strict criteria remains ethically defensible given the documented progressive myelopathy and cord signal changes; I remain concerned that any delay risks irreversible damage.
Whether preoperative biopsy of the C6 lesion is advisable given the potential for bleeding or seeding, versus proceeding directly to surgical resection with intraoperative diagnosis.
The clinical significance of the unexplained left S1-distribution sensory loss and whether it requires separate investigation or intervention before addressing the cervical lesion.
The apparent mismatch between the reported weakness and the normal power on examination; this needs clarification before assigning operative risk and prognosis.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should the tumor board review be scheduled only after all ordered tests are available, or should we convene now with preliminary images and reports if the resident can obtain them?
If the contrast MRI and CT show no aggressive features but confirm severe stenosis, do you agree we can proceed directly to decompression without a preoperative biopsy?
Who should be included in the tumor board beyond spine surgery, radiology, and pathology — for example, medical oncology or interventional radiology?

I accept that we must exclude a vascular or aggressive lesion and understand the left S1 sensory loss before finalizing the approach. I will coordinate the tumor board and provide advice on biopsy and embolization once the contrast MRI and CT are available. I will also ensure the original images are obtained for grading.

director_rulings.public_message: I have heard the arguments from both the rehabilitation physician and the deputy director. I agree that the progressive cervical myelopathy with cord signal change makes surgery strongly indicated, but I am not yet ready to issue a final ruling because several diagnostic ambiguities require clarification and I want to honor our shared decision-making process. Specifically, I ask the resident and radiologist: can you obtain the original images and give us a stenosis grade and lesion characterization, including any suspicion of vascularity or aggressive features? I ask the neurologist to clarify the left S1 sensory loss with an EMG/NCS and to reconcile the reported weakness with the normal examination. I ask the anesthesiologist to complete an airway assessment for prone positioning. I ask the physiatrist to provide a concrete rehabilitation protocol with criteria for immediate surgical referral, so we can compare it against primary surgery with full information. Finally, I ask the vice_director to coordinate a tumor board review and advise whether preoperative biopsy or embolization is needed. I have ordered the following tests now: cervical MRI with contrast, lumbar MRI, dynamic flexion-extension films, and lower limb EMG/NCS. If these investigations reveal a separate compressive lesion or a highly vascular bony tumor, our surgical plan and timing will change accordingly; we will not proceed without resolving these points. We will reconvene once this information is available.

director_rulings.final_decision: We will proceed with additional workup before finalizing treatment. The ordered investigations (cervical MRI with contrast, lumbar MRI, dynamic flexion-extension films, lower limb EMG/NCS) will be completed, and the tumor board will convene once results are available. Surgical decompression is currently indicated given progressive cervical myelopathy and cord signal changes, but the exact approach and timing depend on the workup. If the workup reveals a separate compressive lesion or a highly vascular lesion, the plan will be adjusted accordingly (e.g., embolization or additional decompression); if no such findings, we will proceed with decompression and resection of the C6 lesion. We will reconvene after the investigations.
delegated_tasks: Resident and radiologist: obtain original images and provide stenosis grade and lesion characterization, including suspicion of vascularity or aggressive features.
Neurologist: complete EMG/NCS interpretation and reconcile reported weakness with normal examination; clarify left S1 sensory loss.
Anesthesiologist: complete airway assessment for prone positioning.
Physiatrist: provide concrete rehabilitation protocol with criteria for immediate surgical referral for comparison against primary surgery.

Vice director: coordinate tumor board review, including decision on timing relative to test availability, composition (radiology, pathology, medical oncology, interventional radiology as appropriate), and advise on preoperative biopsy versus direct resection and potential embolization.
director_rulings.reason_for_delay: Awaiting results of ordered investigations and tumor board review to finalize surgical plan and timing; proceeding without resolving the diagnostic ambiguities (possible vascular lesion, separate compressive lesion, unexplained left S1 findings) could lead to an inappropriate approach or avoidable risk.
director_rulings.public_message: We have heard all perspectives and remain committed to a thorough shared decision. The evidence strongly suggests surgery is indicated for progressive cervical myelopathy, but several diagnostic questions must be answered to choose the safest timing and technique. We will complete the ordered investigations and convene the tumor board before finalizing the operative plan. Contingencies are in place: if a separate compressive lesion or a highly vascular tumor is found, we will adjust accordingly. We will reconvene once results are available.
